what-is-ai.prompt: What best describes how most of today's AI systems work?

choices.text: They follow a fixed set of hand-written rules for every situation.
choices.feedback: That's classic rule-based software. Modern AI learns patterns from data instead of being told every rule.

choices.text: They learn statistical patterns from large amounts of example data.
choices.feedback: Right — today's AI is pattern-matching at scale, not hand-coded logic.

choices.text: They are conscious and understand meaning the way people do.
choices.feedback: No — they model patterns in data. There's no understanding or awareness behind the output.

what-is-ai.prompt: A model that writes fluent text must therefore understand what it's saying. True?

choices.text: True — fluency requires comprehension.
choices.feedback: Fluency comes from predicting likely next tokens. A model can be confidently, fluently wrong.

choices.text: False — fluency is pattern prediction, not understanding.
choices.feedback: Exactly. Sounding right and being right are different things.

what-is-ai.prompt: Your phone's face unlock, a chess engine, and ChatGPT are all called "AI". What do they actually share?

choices.text: They all learn patterns from examples rather than following only hand-written rules.
choices.feedback: Right — wildly different jobs, same underlying move: fit patterns from data instead of coding every case by hand.

choices.text: They all understand language.
choices.feedback: Face unlock never touches language. What unites them is learning from data, not any one ability.

choices.text: They all run on the same model.
choices.feedback: They're completely different systems — the shared part is the approach (learning from examples), not the software.

data-and-datasets.prompt: Why does "garbage in, garbage out" matter so much for AI?

choices.text: Models mostly inherit the patterns — and flaws — of the data they're trained on.
choices.feedback: Yes. A model is a mirror of its training data, biases and gaps included.

choices.text: Because more data always makes a model worse.
choices.feedback: Not quantity itself — it's the quality and representativeness of the data that matter.

choices.text: Because models ignore their training data once deployed.
choices.feedback: They don't — everything they 'know' was shaped by that data.

data-and-datasets.prompt: A hiring model is trained only on résumés the company accepted in the past. What's the risk?

choices.text: None — past decisions are the best guide to future ones.
choices.feedback: That's exactly the trap. If past decisions were biased, the model learns the bias as if it were a rule.

choices.text: The model inherits whatever biases shaped those past decisions.
choices.feedback: Yes. The dataset isn't neutral ground truth — it's a record of old judgments, flaws included.

choices.text: The model will refuse to make predictions on new résumés.
choices.feedback: It will happily predict — that's the problem. It just predicts the past, biases and all.

data-and-datasets.prompt: Why do teams spend more time cleaning data than designing models?

choices.text: Because models are already perfect and can't be improved.
choices.feedback: Models improve constantly — but even the best one can't overcome mislabeled, skewed, or missing data.

choices.text: Because data quality usually limits performance more than model choice does.
choices.feedback: Right — a decent model on clean, representative data beats a brilliant model on garbage almost every time.

choices.text: Because cleaning data is required by law.
choices.feedback: Some domains have data regulations, but the real driver is practical: bad data caps what any model can do.

statistics-essentials.prompt: An AI predicts a 70% chance of rain. What does that 70% best represent?

choices.text: It will definitely rain on 70% of the map.
choices.feedback: Probability isn't area — it's a degree of confidence about the outcome.

choices.text: A measure of the model's confidence, not a guarantee.
choices.feedback: Right — it's an estimate of likelihood, and roughly 30% of such days it should be dry.

choices.text: The model is 70% finished computing the answer.
choices.feedback: Probability describes the prediction, not how far along the computation is.

statistics-essentials.prompt: A tool claims "95% accuracy" on detecting a disease that affects 1 in 100 people. Why be careful?

choices.text: Because a model that just says "healthy" every time is already 99% accurate.
choices.feedback: Exactly — with rare events, accuracy alone can hide a model that never catches the thing you care about.

choices.text: Because 95% is a suspiciously low number.
choices.feedback: It's not the number itself — it's that accuracy is misleading when one outcome is far more common than the other.

choices.text: Because accuracy can't be measured on medical data.
choices.feedback: It can be measured fine. The issue is what it hides: rare-event performance needs different metrics.

statistics-essentials.prompt: What does it mean when two measurements are "correlated"?

choices.text: One causes the other.
choices.feedback: Not necessarily — correlation only says they move together. Cause is a separate, harder question.

choices.text: They tend to move together, for whatever reason.
choices.feedback: Right — together says nothing about why. A third factor, coincidence, or causation could all explain it.

choices.text: They are equal.
choices.feedback: Correlated variables can be on completely different scales — they just rise and fall in a related way.

probability-and-uncertainty.prompt: A model gives an answer with high confidence. Can it still be wrong?

choices.text: No — high confidence means it's correct.
choices.feedback: Confidence is the model's own estimate; it can be confidently, fluently wrong.

choices.text: Yes — confidence and correctness are different things.
choices.feedback: Exactly. Whether confidence actually matches accuracy (calibration) is its own hard problem.

probability-and-uncertainty.prompt: Why do modern AI systems output probabilities instead of just answers?

choices.text: Because probabilities look more scientific.
choices.feedback: It's not decoration — the probability carries real information about how much to trust the answer.

choices.text: Because the world is messy, and expressing uncertainty is more honest than pretending to be sure.
choices.feedback: Right — a model that says "70% spam" gives you something a flat "spam" can't: a basis for deciding when to double-check.

choices.text: Because computers can't output words.
choices.feedback: They output words constantly. Probabilities are a choice — a way to communicate confidence, not a limitation.

probability-and-uncertainty.prompt: A weather model said 90% chance of sun, and it rained. Was the model wrong?

choices.text: Yes — it predicted sun and got rain.
choices.feedback: A 90% forecast expects rain 1 time in 10. One rainy day can't tell you the model failed — only many forecasts can.

choices.text: Not necessarily — 90% means rain should still happen about 1 time in 10.
choices.feedback: Exactly. Single outcomes can't judge a probability. What matters is whether its "90%" days come true about 9 times in 10.

choices.text: Models can never be evaluated.
choices.feedback: They can — you check calibration across many predictions, not one. That's the whole trick of judging probabilistic claims.

correlation-vs-causation.prompt: A model notices ice-cream sales and drownings rise together. What's the safe conclusion?

choices.text: Ice cream causes drowning.
choices.feedback: The classic trap. A shared cause — hot weather — drives both.

choices.text: They're correlated, but one may not cause the other.
choices.feedback: Right — correlation is a pattern; causation needs more than co-occurrence.

choices.text: Drowning causes ice-cream sales.
choices.feedback: Reversing the arrow doesn't fix it — correlation alone can't tell you direction.

correlation-vs-causation.prompt: Cities with more firefighters have more fires. Should we cut firefighters to reduce fires?

choices.text: Yes — the data clearly shows firefighters cause fires.
choices.feedback: Careful — big cities have both more fires and more firefighters. Size drives both; that's a confounder, not a cause.

choices.text: No — a third factor (city size) likely drives both numbers.
choices.feedback: Right — this is the classic confounder pattern. The two rise together because something else pushes both up.

choices.text: The data must be fabricated.
choices.feedback: The data can be perfectly real — the error would be in the causal story we tell about it.

correlation-vs-causation.prompt: What's the most reliable way to establish that X actually causes Y?

choices.text: Find a strong correlation in a large dataset.
choices.feedback: Size doesn't fix it — a confounder correlates just as strongly in a big dataset as a small one.

choices.text: Run an experiment: change X deliberately and watch what happens to Y.
choices.feedback: Right — intervening is what separates cause from mere association. It's why randomized trials are the gold standard.

choices.text: Ask a language model whether X causes Y.
choices.feedback: A model can summarize what's known, but it can't establish causation from observational patterns any better than we can.

patterns-and-predictions.prompt: At its core, generating text from a language model is closest to which task?

choices.text: Looking the answer up in a stored database of facts.
choices.feedback: There's no lookup table — it predicts, it doesn't retrieve (unless you bolt retrieval on).

choices.text: Predicting the next most-likely piece of text, step by step.
choices.feedback: Yes — it's sequential next-token prediction, one piece at a time.

choices.text: Running a formal logical proof to derive the answer.
choices.feedback: It approximates reasoning through patterns; it isn't executing formal logic.

patterns-and-predictions.prompt: Your keyboard suggests the next word as you type. A language model writes an essay. How different are these?

choices.text: Fundamentally the same mechanism — predict the next piece of text — at very different scales.
choices.feedback: Right — the essay-writer is next-word prediction scaled up enormously, with far more context and far richer patterns.

choices.text: Completely different — one predicts, the other thinks.
choices.feedback: Tempting, but the essay is produced word by word by the same core move: predict what comes next.

choices.text: The keyboard is more advanced because it's faster.
choices.feedback: Speed isn't sophistication — the language model considers vastly more context per prediction.

patterns-and-predictions.prompt: Why can a system trained only to predict end up looking creative?

choices.text: Because prediction over rich enough patterns can recombine them in ways nobody wrote down.
choices.feedback: Yes — learn deep patterns of how ideas connect, and novel-seeming combinations fall out of prediction itself.

choices.text: Because someone secretly adds creativity as a separate module.
choices.feedback: There's no creativity module — the surprising outputs emerge from pattern prediction at scale.

choices.text: It can't — anything that predicts is just copying.
choices.feedback: It doesn't copy — it generates new sequences that follow learned patterns. That's why outputs aren't in the training data verbatim.

choices.text: A set of learned numbers (parameters) that map inputs to outputs.
choices.feedback: Right — training tunes those weights; the model is those numbers plus its architecture.

choices.text: A physical robot or server.
choices.feedback: Hardware runs the model, but the model itself is the learned parameters.

choices.text: A copy of the internet stored word-for-word.
choices.feedback: It doesn't store text verbatim — it compresses patterns into weights.

what-is-a-model.prompt: After training finishes, what do you actually have on disk?

choices.text: A database of all the training examples.
choices.feedback: The examples are gone — what remains is what was distilled from them: millions or billions of tuned numbers.

choices.text: A huge collection of numbers (weights) that encode the learned patterns.
choices.feedback: Right — a model is, concretely, a file of numbers plus the recipe for using them. Nothing more mystical than that.

choices.text: A program with hand-written rules for every case.
choices.feedback: Nobody wrote the rules — the numbers were tuned automatically until the outputs looked right.

what-is-a-model.prompt: Why is "the map is not the territory" a useful way to think about models?

choices.text: Because models literally contain maps.
choices.feedback: It's a metaphor — the point is that a model is a simplified stand-in for reality, not reality itself.

choices.text: Because a model is a simplification of the world, useful precisely because it leaves things out.
choices.feedback: Right — and like a map, it's reliable where it was drawn well and misleading where it wasn't.

choices.text: Because bigger models are always more accurate maps.
choices.feedback: Bigger helps but doesn't guarantee accuracy — a huge model of bad data is a detailed map of the wrong territory.

bias-in-data.prompt: Where does most harmful bias in AI systems originate?

choices.text: Patterns and imbalances in the training data and its labels.
choices.feedback: Yes — models absorb the skews of their data and how it was labelled.

choices.text: Random electrical noise in the hardware.
choices.feedback: Bias is systematic, not random noise — it traces back to data and design choices.

choices.text: The user's phrasing, and nothing else.
choices.feedback: Phrasing can surface bias, but the bias was learned from data first.

bias-in-data.prompt: A face-recognition system works worse on darker skin tones. What's the most likely root cause?

choices.text: The camera hardware is racist.
choices.feedback: Hardware can contribute (poor low-light calibration), but the dominant cause is usually training data that under-represents some groups.

choices.text: The training data contained far fewer examples of darker-skinned faces.
choices.feedback: Right — models perform worst where they saw least. Unrepresentative data becomes unequal performance.

choices.text: Face recognition is impossible for some skin tones.
choices.feedback: It's not impossible — systems trained on balanced data close most of the gap. The failure was in the dataset.

bias-in-data.prompt: Can you fix biased data by simply deleting the sensitive column (race, gender)?

choices.text: Yes — if the model can't see it, it can't use it.
choices.feedback: Unfortunately no — zip code, name, school, and dozens of other fields can act as proxies for the deleted column.

choices.text: No — other features often act as proxies that leak the same information.
choices.feedback: Right — this is why "fairness through blindness" fails. The signal hides in correlated features.

choices.text: Yes, but only for small datasets.
choices.feedback: Size doesn't matter here — proxies leak the information at any scale.

features-and-labels.prompt: In supervised learning, what is a "label"?

choices.text: The correct answer the model is trained to predict.
choices.feedback: Right — features are the inputs, the label is the target answer.

choices.text: The name of the dataset file.
choices.feedback: That's just a filename — a label is the ground-truth output for each example.

choices.text: A tag the model invents entirely on its own.
choices.feedback: Labels are supplied by humans or a process; inventing them is unsupervised territory.

features-and-labels.prompt: You're building a spam filter. Which of these is the label?

choices.text: The email's subject line.
choices.feedback: That's a feature — an input the model reads. The label is the answer we want it to learn: spam or not.

choices.text: Whether the email is spam or not.
choices.feedback: Right — the label is the answer key. Features describe the example; the label is what you're trying to predict.

choices.text: The model's accuracy score.
choices.feedback: Accuracy measures the model after training — it's not part of the training examples at all.

features-and-labels.prompt: Where do labels usually come from?

choices.text: The model generates them itself during training.
choices.feedback: In supervised learning the labels must exist before training — the model learns by comparing its guesses against them.

choices.text: Humans annotate them, or they're harvested from existing records — often the most expensive part of the project.
choices.feedback: Right — labeling is slow, human work, which is why labeled data is precious and companies guard it.

choices.text: They're downloaded free with any dataset.
choices.feedback: Sometimes labels come attached, but high-quality labels for your specific problem usually have to be made — at real cost.

training-vs-testing.prompt: Why hold out a separate test set the model never trains on?

choices.text: To check whether it generalises, not just memorises.
choices.feedback: Exactly — testing on training data flatters the model and hides overfitting.

choices.text: To give the model more data to learn from.
choices.feedback: The test set is deliberately withheld — learning from it defeats its purpose.

choices.text: Because testing is faster than training.
choices.feedback: Speed isn't the point — an honest estimate of real-world performance is.

training-vs-testing.prompt: A student memorizes last year's exam answers, then aces a retake of that same exam. What did we learn about the student?

choices.text: They've mastered the subject.
choices.feedback: We can't tell — they might only know those exact answers. Same with models: training-set scores can't reveal memorization.

choices.text: Almost nothing — we need to test them on questions they haven't seen.
choices.feedback: Exactly — that's the whole argument for a held-out test set. Only unseen questions measure real understanding.

choices.text: They cheated.
choices.feedback: Not necessarily cheating — but the score is meaningless as a measure of understanding. New questions are the only honest test.

choices.text: When training data accidentally contains information from the test set.
choices.feedback: Right — the exam answers leaked into the study materials. Scores look great; real-world performance won't be.

choices.text: When a dataset file gets corrupted.
choices.feedback: That's just data loss. Leakage is subtler — test information sneaking into training, inflating scores.

choices.text: When a model shares its weights publicly.
choices.feedback: That's open-sourcing, not leakage. Leakage is test-set contamination that makes evaluation dishonest.

overfitting-underfitting.prompt: A model scores 99% on its training data but 60% on new data. What's happening?

choices.text: Underfitting — the model is too simple.
choices.feedback: Underfitting scores poorly on both. The big gap points the other way.

choices.text: Overfitting — it memorised the training set instead of generalising.
choices.feedback: Right — a large train/test gap is the signature of overfitting.

choices.text: Perfect generalisation.
choices.feedback: Generalisation means close scores on both; a 39-point gap is the opposite.

choices.text: The model is too simple to capture the real pattern — bad on training data and new data alike.
choices.feedback: Right — it's the opposite failure to overfitting: the model couldn't even memorize, let alone generalize.

choices.text: The model memorized the training data.
choices.feedback: That's overfitting. Underfitting is when the model is too weak to capture the pattern at all — it fails everywhere.

choices.text: The model was trained on too much data.
choices.feedback: More data doesn't cause underfitting — an overly simple model or too little training does.

overfitting-underfitting.prompt: How do practitioners usually detect overfitting during training?

choices.text: Training loss keeps improving while validation loss starts getting worse.
choices.feedback: Right — that widening gap is the classic signature: the model is memorizing the training set instead of learning the pattern.

choices.text: The model starts running slower.
choices.feedback: Speed doesn't change with overfitting — the tell is in the metrics: training keeps improving while held-out performance decays.

choices.text: The loss becomes exactly zero on all data.
choices.feedback: Zero loss on everything would be suspicious perfection — the real signal is divergence between training and validation curves.

neural-networks.prompt: What does a single artificial "neuron" actually do?

choices.text: Stores one fact, like a row in a spreadsheet.
choices.feedback: Neurons don't store facts — they compute a weighted sum and pass it through a function.

choices.text: Takes weighted inputs, sums them, and applies an activation function.
choices.feedback: Yes — stack millions of these and the network learns patterns.

choices.text: Makes the final yes/no decision for the whole network.
choices.feedback: At most that's the output layer's job; one neuron is a tiny building block.

choices.text: Many layers stacked, each building on the patterns the previous one found.
choices.feedback: Right — depth is layers. Early ones catch simple patterns, later ones compose them into increasingly abstract concepts.

choices.text: It runs deep underground for cooling.
choices.feedback: The depth is architectural, not physical — it counts layers of neurons, each transforming the previous layer's output.

choices.text: It uses very large numbers.
choices.feedback: The numbers are ordinary — depth means many stacked layers, which is what lets simple units express complex functions.

neural-networks.prompt: One neuron is trivial. A billion connected neurons can write poetry. What explains the leap?

choices.text: At scale, some neurons become intelligent.
choices.feedback: No individual neuron ever gets smarter — the capability lives in the connections and their learned weights, not in any unit.

choices.text: Simple units, composed in layers and tuned by training, add up to behavior none of them has alone.
choices.feedback: Right — it's emergence through composition. The intelligence is in the arrangement, the same way no single brain cell understands language.

choices.text: Poetry was directly programmed into the network.
choices.feedback: Nobody programmed poems — the network learned patterns of language from data, and composition at scale did the rest.

gradient-descent.prompt: Gradient descent improves a model by…

choices.text: randomly guessing weights until one happens to work.
choices.feedback: It's not random — the gradient points toward weights that reduce the error.

choices.text: nudging weights in the direction that lowers the loss, step by step.
choices.feedback: Right — follow the slope downhill on the loss surface, repeatedly.

choices.text: deleting the worst training examples.
choices.feedback: It adjusts the weights, not the dataset.

gradient-descent.prompt: The classic metaphor: gradient descent is like walking downhill in fog. What's the "hill"?

choices.text: The loss surface — how wrong the model is at every possible setting of its weights.
choices.feedback: Right — each point on the landscape is one configuration of weights; altitude is error. Training walks downhill toward less wrong.

choices.text: The physical server room.
choices.feedback: The hill is mathematical — a landscape where position means weight values and height means error.

choices.text: The amount of training data.
choices.feedback: Data shapes the landscape, but the hill itself is the loss as a function of the model's weights.

gradient-descent.prompt: Why does the learning rate (step size) matter in gradient descent?

choices.text: It doesn't — any step size reaches the same place.
choices.feedback: It matters a lot: steps too big bounce over the valley; too small and training crawls or stalls in a dip.

choices.text: Too large overshoots the minimum; too small crawls or gets stuck.
choices.feedback: Right — it's one of the most fiddly knobs in training. The art is a step size that descends briskly without leaping past the low point.

choices.text: Larger is always better because training finishes faster.
choices.feedback: Faster per step, but big steps can leap over the valley entirely and never settle — speed isn't convergence.

tokenization.prompt: Before a language model reads your text, what happens first?

choices.text: It's split into tokens — chunks like words or word-pieces — mapped to numbers.
choices.feedback: Yes — models operate on token IDs, not raw letters.

choices.text: It's translated into English.
choices.feedback: There's no translation step — it's tokenized in whatever language it's in.

choices.text: It's checked and corrected for spelling.
choices.feedback: No spell-check stage — the text is simply tokenized.

tokenization.prompt: Why can a common word and a rare word cost different numbers of tokens?

choices.text: Rare or unusual words get split into several sub-word pieces.
choices.feedback: Right — frequent words are often one token; rare ones fragment into many.

choices.text: Longer words are always exactly one token.
choices.feedback: Length doesn't guarantee one token — rare strings split into pieces.

choices.text: Tokens are counted one per character, always.
choices.feedback: Most modern tokenizers use sub-words, not single characters.

tokenization.prompt: Why do language models sometimes struggle to count the letters in a word like "strawberry"?

choices.text: They never see letters — they see tokens, and "strawberry" may be one or two chunks with no letter-level view.
choices.feedback: Right — the model's atoms are tokens, not characters. Asking it to count letters is asking about a level it literally never observes.

choices.text: Berries are underrepresented in training data.
choices.feedback: It's not about fruit — it's that tokenization hides individual letters from the model entirely.

choices.text: Counting requires a calculator plugin.
choices.feedback: The deeper issue is representational: the model reads chunked tokens, so letters inside a chunk are invisible to it.

choices.text: A list of numbers (a vector) that captures the meaning of a piece of text.
choices.feedback: Yes — similar meanings land near each other in that vector space.

choices.text: A compressed image file.
choices.feedback: Embeddings are numeric vectors for meaning, not an image format.

choices.text: The raw text, stored exactly as written.
choices.feedback: It's a learned numeric representation, not the original text.

embeddings.prompt: In embedding space, "king" and "queen" end up close together because…

choices.text: they're spelled similarly.
choices.feedback: Spelling isn't it — 'king' and 'kindle' look alike but mean different things.

choices.text: they appear in similar contexts, so they get similar vectors.
choices.feedback: Right — meaning comes from usage patterns, captured as nearby vectors.

choices.text: they have the same number of letters.
choices.feedback: Letter count has nothing to do with embeddings.

embeddings.prompt: How does semantic search use embeddings to beat keyword search?

choices.text: It matches by meaning — "how do I fix a flat" finds "repairing a punctured tyre" despite sharing no words.
choices.feedback: Right — both phrases land close together in embedding space, so nearness finds what keywords miss.

choices.text: It searches faster than keyword search.
choices.feedback: Speed isn't the point — meaning is. Embeddings find matches that share no words at all, because they're near in meaning-space.

choices.text: It corrects your spelling first.
choices.feedback: Spell-check is separate — the real trick is that similar meanings get similar vectors, so distance measures relatedness.

transformers.prompt: What key idea made transformers so effective for language?

choices.text: An attention mechanism that weighs the relationships between all tokens.
choices.feedback: Yes — attention lets each token look at every other token in context.

choices.text: Reading text strictly one word at a time, like older RNNs.
choices.feedback: That's the older approach transformers replaced; attention sees the whole context at once.

choices.text: Storing the entire internet to look answers up.
choices.feedback: No lookup store — they learn weighted patterns through attention.

transformers.prompt: In a transformer, "attention" lets a token…

choices.text: decide which other tokens matter most for interpreting it.
choices.feedback: Right — attention assigns learned weights to other tokens' relevance.

choices.text: pay exactly equal attention to every token, always.
choices.feedback: The whole point is unequal, learned weighting — not uniform attention.

choices.text: ignore all of the other tokens.
choices.feedback: The opposite — attention is about relating tokens to each other.

transformers.prompt: Before transformers, models read text one word at a time in order. What did transformers change?

choices.text: They process all tokens in parallel, letting every word relate to every other word at once.
choices.feedback: Right — parallelism made training dramatically faster and let the architecture scale, which is half the story of modern AI.

choices.text: They read text backwards instead.
choices.feedback: Not backwards — all at once. Every token attends to every other simultaneously instead of waiting in line.

choices.text: They eliminated the need for training.
choices.feedback: Training is still everything — transformers just made it parallelizable enough to scale to enormous datasets.

attention.prompt: In "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big", attention helps the model figure out…

choices.text: what "it" refers to, by weighing the surrounding words.
choices.feedback: Exactly — attention links 'it' to 'trophy' using the context.

choices.text: the correct spelling of "suitcase".
choices.feedback: Attention is about relationships in meaning, not spelling.

choices.text: nothing — pronouns are skipped entirely.
choices.feedback: Resolving references like this is precisely what attention is good at.

attention.prompt: Why does attention use three roles — queries, keys, and values?

choices.text: It's like a lookup: each token asks a question (query), others advertise what they offer (key), and the matches contribute their content (value).
choices.feedback: Right — the query-key match decides who's relevant; the values are what actually flows through. A soft, learned lookup table.

choices.text: Three was chosen arbitrarily and any number works the same.
choices.feedback: The three roles are functionally distinct — asking, matching, and delivering content. Remove one and the mechanism stops making sense.

choices.text: They encrypt the text for security.
choices.feedback: No encryption involved — keys here are lookup keys, as in a dictionary, not cryptographic keys.

attention.prompt: What does "multi-head" attention buy you over a single attention head?

choices.text: Each head can track a different kind of relationship — grammar in one, meaning in another — simultaneously.
choices.feedback: Right — one head might follow pronouns, another subject-verb links. Multiple lenses on the same sentence, all at once.

choices.text: It's purely a marketing term.
choices.feedback: It's mechanical, not marketing — separate heads learn genuinely different relationship patterns, visible when you inspect them.

choices.text: More heads mean the model reads more documents.
choices.feedback: Heads don't add reading capacity — they add parallel perspectives on the same text.

choices.text: The maximum amount of text it can consider at once.
choices.feedback: Right — beyond that limit, earlier content falls out of view.

choices.text: The size of your browser window.
choices.feedback: It's a token limit inside the model, not anything on your screen.

choices.text: How long the model spent training.
choices.feedback: That's training time; the context window is about input length at inference.

context-windows.prompt: You paste a 300-page contract into a model with a small context window. What actually happens?

choices.text: Whatever doesn't fit is simply not seen — the model answers from the part that fit.
choices.feedback: Right — nothing outside the window exists for the model. Confident answers about unseen pages are a classic failure to watch for.

choices.text: The model reads it in installments and remembers each one.
choices.feedback: There's no memory between calls — anything beyond the window is gone, not postponed.

choices.text: The model slows down but reads everything.
choices.feedback: It's a hard limit, not a speed issue — tokens past the boundary are never processed at all.

context-windows.prompt: Why doesn't every model just ship with a giant context window?

choices.text: Attention cost grows steeply with length, and models often use very long contexts poorly anyway.
choices.feedback: Right — longer windows cost real compute, and "lost in the middle" shows models can neglect content buried deep in a long prompt.

choices.text: Regulations cap the window size.
choices.feedback: No law involved — the constraints are compute cost and how well the model actually uses distant tokens.

choices.text: Long documents are copyrighted.
choices.feedback: Copyright isn't the issue — the trade-offs are computational cost and attention quality over long spans.

temperature-sampling.prompt: Raising the "temperature" when generating text does what?

choices.text: Makes the output more random and varied.
choices.feedback: Yes — higher temperature flattens the odds, so less-likely tokens appear more often.

choices.text: Makes the hardware physically run hotter.
choices.feedback: It's a sampling parameter, not hardware heat.

choices.text: Guarantees more factual answers.
choices.feedback: Higher temperature usually means less predictable output, not more accurate.

temperature-sampling.prompt: You want a model to extract data into a fixed format. What temperature setting makes sense?

choices.text: Low (near 0) — you want the most likely, most consistent output, not creative variation.
choices.feedback: Right — extraction, classification, code: turn the dial down. Save high temperature for brainstorming and prose.

choices.text: As high as possible for maximum intelligence.
choices.feedback: Temperature doesn't add intelligence — it adds randomness. For structured tasks, randomness is just error.

choices.text: Temperature doesn't affect output at all.
choices.feedback: It directly shapes sampling: low sharpens toward the likeliest tokens, high flattens toward variety.

temperature-sampling.prompt: At temperature 0, is the model's answer guaranteed correct?

choices.text: No — it's just the model's most probable answer, which can still be confidently wrong.
choices.feedback: Right — temperature 0 buys consistency, not truth. The most likely token sequence can be a fluent mistake.

choices.text: Yes — zero randomness means zero errors.
choices.feedback: Randomness and wrongness are different things — determinism just means it makes the same mistake every time.

choices.text: Temperature 0 disables the model.
choices.feedback: It runs fine — it simply always picks the highest-probability token instead of sampling.

prompt-engineering.prompt: Why does giving a model an example or two in the prompt often help?

choices.text: It demonstrates the format and task, steering the next prediction.
choices.feedback: Right — in-context examples shape what the model produces next.

choices.text: It permanently retrains the model's weights.
choices.feedback: Prompting doesn't change weights — the effect lasts only for that request.

choices.text: It makes the model run faster.
choices.feedback: Examples affect quality and format, not speed — they can even cost more tokens.

prompt-engineering.prompt: What's the single highest-leverage fix for a vague, unhelpful model response?

choices.text: Add specifics: the context, the audience, the format you want, and an example if you have one.
choices.feedback: Right — most "bad model" moments are underspecified prompts. Specificity converts guesswork into instruction-following.

choices.text: Type the same prompt again in all caps.
choices.feedback: Emphasis isn't information — what the model lacks is specifics: context, audience, format, examples.

choices.text: Switch to a bigger model immediately.
choices.feedback: Sometimes needed, but a sharper prompt on the same model usually beats the same vague prompt on a bigger one.

prompt-engineering.prompt: Why does telling the model who the answer is for ("explain to a lawyer" vs "to a 10-year-old") change so much?

choices.text: It concentrates the model on the register, vocabulary, and assumptions appropriate to that audience.
choices.feedback: Right — audience is one of the strongest signals you can give: it collapses thousands of possible framings down to the right one.

choices.text: The model verifies the reader's identity.
choices.feedback: No verification — the audience cue steers style and depth, selecting which patterns of explanation to draw on.

choices.text: It doesn't — output is audience-independent.
choices.feedback: Try it both ways — tone, vocabulary, and structure shift dramatically. Audience framing is leverage.

rag.prompt: What problem does Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mainly solve?

choices.text: Giving the model relevant, up-to-date facts it wasn't trained on.
choices.feedback: Yes — retrieve documents, then let the model answer grounded in them.

choices.text: Making the model retrain itself overnight.
choices.feedback: RAG adds context at query time; it doesn't retrain anything.

choices.text: Removing the need for a model at all.
choices.feedback: RAG feeds a model — it doesn't replace one.

rag.prompt: In RAG, where do the retrieved documents go?

choices.text: Into the model's prompt/context for that single answer.
choices.feedback: Right — they're injected as context, not baked into the weights.

choices.text: Permanently into the model's parameters.
choices.feedback: Nothing is written to the weights — retrieval happens per request.

choices.text: They replace the user's question.
choices.feedback: They supplement the question as supporting context, not replace it.

rag.prompt: Even with perfect retrieval, RAG can still fail. How?

choices.text: The model can ignore, misread, or override the retrieved passages with its own priors.
choices.feedback: Right — retrieval puts the truth in the context; generation still has to use it. Grounding failures are RAG's second half.

choices.text: It can't — correct documents guarantee correct answers.
choices.feedback: The generator can still contradict its sources or blend them wrongly — faithful use of retrieved text is its own problem.

choices.text: Only if the internet goes down.
choices.feedback: RAG often runs on local indexes — the deeper failure mode is the model mishandling what retrieval found.

hallucination.prompt: Why do language models sometimes "hallucinate" confident but false statements?

choices.text: They generate plausible-sounding text, and plausible isn't always true.
choices.feedback: Exactly — they optimise for likely continuations, not verified facts.

choices.text: Someone manually typed the wrong answer in.
choices.feedback: No human typed it — the model produced a fluent guess.

choices.text: They always know when they're unsure and say so.
choices.feedback: They often don't — confidence and correctness can come apart.

hallucination.prompt: Why does a model hallucinate a plausible-sounding citation instead of saying "I don't know"?

choices.text: It's trained to continue text plausibly — a well-formed fake citation is high-probability text, and "I don't know" often isn't.
choices.feedback: Right — the model completes patterns. Citations have a strong pattern; the training pressure toward fluent continuation beats abstention.

choices.text: It's deliberately lying to please you.
choices.feedback: There's no intent — it's pattern completion. The fake reference is what statistically-likely text looks like, not a chosen deception.

choices.text: Its database of citations is corrupted.
choices.feedback: There is no citation database — it generates text token by token, and reference-shaped text is easy to generate whether or not it's real.

hallucination.prompt: Which habit best protects you from hallucinations in practice?

choices.text: Verify anything specific and consequential — names, numbers, citations, quotes — against a primary source.
choices.feedback: Right — treat the model as a brilliant but unreliable colleague. Specifics that matter get checked; that habit catches most damage.

choices.text: Ask the model "are you sure?" and trust its yes.
choices.feedback: Models often double down as fluently as they erred — self-confirmation isn't verification.

choices.text: Only use models at night.
choices.feedback: Time of day changes nothing — the reliable defense is independently checking consequential specifics.

loss-functions.prompt: What does a loss function measure during training?

choices.text: How far the model's predictions are from the right answers.
choices.feedback: Right — training works to make that number smaller.

choices.text: How fast the model runs.
choices.feedback: That's speed/latency, not loss. Loss is about prediction error.

choices.text: How much memory the model uses.
choices.feedback: That's resource usage — loss measures how wrong the predictions are.

loss-functions.prompt: Why does the choice of loss function matter so much?

choices.text: It defines what "wrong" means — and the model becomes whatever minimizes it, side effects included.
choices.feedback: Right — the loss is the objective, literally. Models are ruthless optimizers of exactly what you wrote down, not what you meant.

choices.text: It only affects training speed.
choices.feedback: It shapes far more than speed — it defines the target. Different losses produce genuinely different models.

choices.text: It doesn't — all loss functions give the same result eventually.
choices.feedback: They don't converge to the same place. Penalize big errors more, and the model behaves differently than if all errors count equally.

loss-functions.prompt: During training, what happens to the loss number if things are going well?

choices.text: It steadily rises.
choices.feedback: Other way around — loss measures error, so learning means driving it down.

choices.text: It steadily falls.
choices.feedback: Right — falling loss means shrinking error. It's the heartbeat researchers watch during every training run.

choices.text: It stays exactly constant.
choices.feedback: Flat loss means nothing is being learned — the whole point of training is to push it down.

regression-classification.prompt: What's the core difference between regression and classification?

choices.text: Regression predicts a number; classification predicts a category.
choices.feedback: Exactly — a price vs a label like spam/not-spam.

choices.text: Regression is for images, classification for text.
choices.feedback: Neither is tied to a data type — the difference is number vs category.

choices.text: They're two names for the same thing.
choices.feedback: They're distinct tasks: continuous values vs discrete classes.

regression-classification.prompt: Predicting tomorrow's temperature vs. predicting whether it will rain — which is which?

choices.text: Temperature is regression (a number); rain-or-not is classification (a category).
choices.feedback: Right — continuous quantity vs. discrete bucket. Same weather, two different problem shapes.

choices.text: Both are classification.
choices.feedback: Rain-or-not is, but temperature is a continuous value — that makes it regression.

choices.text: Both are regression.
choices.feedback: Temperature is, but rain-or-not has two buckets — that's classification.

regression-classification.prompt: A model predicts house prices. Someone suggests converting it to predict "cheap / medium / expensive" instead. What changed?

choices.text: Nothing meaningful.
choices.feedback: Something real changed: a continuous target became categories. You lose precision but sometimes gain robustness and interpretability.

choices.text: The problem went from regression to classification — trading precision for simpler buckets.
choices.feedback: Right — same data, reframed problem. The framing decides what the model can tell you.

choices.text: The model became more accurate automatically.
choices.feedback: Not automatically — buckets are easier to hit but say less. It's a trade-off, not a free win.

clustering.prompt: Clustering is an example of which kind of learning?

choices.text: Unsupervised — it groups data without labels.
choices.feedback: Right — it finds structure on its own, no answer key.

choices.text: Supervised — it needs labelled examples.
choices.feedback: No labels required — that's what makes clustering unsupervised.

choices.text: Reinforcement — it learns from rewards.
choices.feedback: No reward signal here; clustering just groups similar points.

clustering.prompt: You have 10,000 customer records and no labels at all. What can clustering give you?

choices.text: Nothing — machine learning requires labels.
choices.feedback: Supervised learning does; clustering doesn't. It finds structure in unlabeled data — that's its whole job.

choices.text: Groups of similar customers you didn't know existed.
choices.feedback: Right — clustering surfaces natural groupings without being told what to look for. Naming the groups is then your job.

choices.text: Exact predictions of what each customer will buy.
choices.feedback: That would need labeled purchase data. Clustering only groups by similarity — interpretation and prediction come after.

clustering.prompt: A clustering algorithm split your data into 5 groups. Are those the "true" groups?

choices.text: Yes — the algorithm found the objective truth.
choices.feedback: There's usually no single truth — different algorithms, distance measures, or a different k give different, equally valid splits.

choices.text: Not necessarily — you often chose the number 5, and different settings give different groupings.
choices.feedback: Right — clusters are a lens, not a fact. Their value is whether they're useful, not whether they're "true".

choices.text: No — clustering results are always random noise.
choices.feedback: They're not noise — real structure does surface. It's just not the unique, objective structure.

evaluation-metrics.prompt: Why isn't raw accuracy always a good metric?

choices.text: On imbalanced data, always guessing the majority class can still score high.
choices.feedback: Exactly — 99% accuracy is meaningless if 99% of cases are one class.

choices.text: Accuracy is always the single best metric.
choices.feedback: It can hide real failure modes — that's the whole point of the question.

choices.text: Accuracy can't be computed for classifiers.
choices.feedback: It can — it's just not always the most informative measure.

evaluation-metrics.prompt: For a cancer-screening model, which error is usually worse?

choices.text: A false negative — telling a sick patient they're healthy.
choices.feedback: Right — a missed cancer can be fatal; a false alarm costs a follow-up test. This asymmetry is why recall matters more than accuracy here.

choices.text: A false positive — flagging a healthy patient.
choices.feedback: It causes stress and extra tests, but a missed cancer is usually far more costly. The metric should reflect that asymmetry.

choices.text: Both errors are always equally bad.
choices.feedback: Rarely true in the real world — the whole craft of choosing metrics is weighing which mistakes hurt more.

evaluation-metrics.prompt: Precision and recall pull against each other. Why?

choices.text: They don't — improving one always improves the other.
choices.feedback: Usually the opposite: flag more aggressively and recall rises while precision falls. There's a dial, and it trades one for the other.

choices.text: Because flagging more things catches more true cases (recall up) but adds more false alarms (precision down).
choices.feedback: Right — it's a threshold trade-off. Where you set the dial depends on which mistake costs more.

choices.text: Because they're computed on different datasets.
choices.feedback: Same dataset, same predictions — the tension comes from the flagging threshold, not the data.

backpropagation.prompt: What does backpropagation do during training?

choices.text: Sends the error backward through the network to update each weight.
choices.feedback: Right — it figures out how much each weight contributed to the error.

choices.text: Generates new training data.
choices.feedback: It adjusts weights using existing data; it doesn't create data.

choices.text: Chooses which examples to train on.
choices.feedback: That's data selection — backprop is about propagating the error to weights.

backpropagation.prompt: Backpropagation works backwards through the network. Backwards from what?

choices.text: From the error at the output, tracing how much each weight contributed to it.
choices.feedback: Right — it starts at the mistake and walks backwards, assigning blame layer by layer so each weight knows how to adjust.

choices.text: From the first layer to the last.
choices.feedback: That's the forward pass — the prediction. Backprop runs the other way, from the output error back toward the input.

choices.text: From the training data to the internet.
choices.feedback: Everything stays inside the network — backprop flows error signals from output back through the layers.

backpropagation.prompt: Why was backpropagation such a breakthrough for deep networks?

choices.text: It made networks conscious.
choices.feedback: No consciousness involved — it solved an accounting problem: how to compute every weight's share of the blame efficiently.

choices.text: It gave an efficient way to compute how every weight, even in deep layers, should change.
choices.feedback: Right — without it, credit assignment in deep networks is hopeless. With it, training a billion weights becomes routine calculus.

choices.text: It removed the need for training data.
choices.feedback: Data is still essential — backprop just makes learning from that data computationally feasible in deep networks.

gpus-and-compute.prompt: Why are GPUs central to modern AI?

choices.text: They do the massively parallel matrix math training needs, far faster than CPUs.
choices.feedback: Right — neural nets are mostly matrix multiplications, which GPUs excel at.

choices.text: They store the training data.
choices.feedback: Storage is disks; GPUs do the heavy parallel computation.

choices.text: They write the model's code.
choices.feedback: They run the math, they don't author code.

gpus-and-compute.prompt: Why is a GPU better than a CPU for training neural networks?

choices.text: GPUs are newer, so they're faster at everything.
choices.feedback: CPUs still win at many tasks — GPUs win specifically at doing thousands of simple calculations simultaneously, which is exactly what neural nets need.

choices.text: Neural nets are mostly huge batches of identical simple math — exactly what a GPU's thousands of cores do in parallel.
choices.feedback: Right — graphics and neural nets share a shape: massive parallel arithmetic. The chip built for one turned out perfect for the other.

choices.text: GPUs have more storage space.
choices.feedback: Storage isn't the bottleneck — parallel throughput is. A GPU's advantage is doing many multiplications at once.

gpus-and-compute.prompt: What does it mean that compute has become a strategic resource in AI?

choices.text: Every laptop can now train frontier models.
choices.feedback: The opposite — frontier training runs need thousands of top-end chips for months, which is why access to compute shapes who can compete.

choices.text: Training frontier models requires so many chips that access to them shapes who can build what.
choices.feedback: Right — chip supply, export controls, and datacenter buildouts are now part of AI geopolitics. Compute is the new oil rig.

choices.text: Computers are getting more expensive to plug in.
choices.feedback: Electricity matters at datacenter scale, but the strategic scarcity is the chips themselves and who can get enough of them.

diffusion.prompt: How does a diffusion model generate an image?

choices.text: It starts from noise and removes it step by step toward a coherent image.
choices.feedback: Right — it learns to reverse a noising process, denoising into an image.

choices.text: It pastes together cropped pieces of training images.
choices.feedback: No collage — it denoises from scratch, it doesn't copy-paste.

choices.text: It looks the image up in a stored database.
choices.feedback: There's no lookup — it generates pixels by iterative denoising.

diffusion.prompt: Diffusion models are trained by destroying images. Why?

choices.text: Learning to undo noise step-by-step teaches the model to build images from pure noise.
choices.feedback: Right — corrupt an image gradually, learn to reverse each step, and generation becomes: start from static, denoise your way to a picture.

choices.text: Destroyed images are cheaper to store.
choices.feedback: Storage isn't it — the destruction creates the training task. Reversing it is the learned skill that powers generation.

choices.text: To remove copyrighted content from them.
choices.feedback: The noising isn't about rights — it's the core training mechanism: learn the reverse of gradual corruption.

diffusion.prompt: Why does image generation take multiple steps while text models emit tokens directly?

choices.text: Diffusion refines the whole image gradually, noise to detail — each step denoises a little more.
choices.feedback: Right — it's iterative refinement of the entire canvas, unlike text's one-token-at-a-time. That's also why fewer steps means faster but rougher.

choices.text: Images are stored in slower databases.
choices.feedback: It's not storage — the multi-step process is intrinsic to how diffusion works: repeated partial denoising.

choices.text: It doesn't — image models are instant.
choices.feedback: Classic diffusion needs dozens of denoising passes; the multi-step nature is fundamental (though distillation is shrinking it).

mixture-of-experts.prompt: What does a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model do?

choices.text: Routes each input to a few specialised sub-networks instead of using the whole model.
choices.feedback: Right — only a fraction of the parameters fire per token, saving compute.

choices.text: Averages the answers of many separate full models.
choices.feedback: That's ensembling — MoE routes within one model to chosen experts.

choices.text: Asks human experts to label the data.
choices.feedback: The 'experts' are sub-networks, not people.

mixture-of-experts.prompt: A 700B-parameter MoE model can run cheaper than a 70B dense model. How?

choices.text: Only a few experts activate per token — most of those 700B parameters sit idle on any given step.
choices.feedback: Right — capacity you store vs. compute you spend become separate dials. The router wakes only the relevant slice.

choices.text: It secretly has fewer parameters than advertised.
choices.feedback: The parameters are real — they're just not all used at once. Sparse activation is the whole trick.

choices.text: It runs on cheaper electricity.
choices.feedback: The saving is architectural — per token, only a fraction of the network computes, so inference costs less than its size suggests.

mixture-of-experts.prompt: What does the "router" in a mixture-of-experts model do?

choices.text: It decides which experts handle each token, learned during training.
choices.feedback: Right — the router is a small learned gatekeeper. Its choices are what make the sparsity work.

choices.text: It connects the model to the internet.
choices.feedback: Not a network router — it routes tokens to internal expert sub-networks.

choices.text: A human operator assigns the experts manually.
choices.feedback: No human in the loop — routing is learned end-to-end and happens per token, millions of times a second.

choices.text: It works across more than one kind of input — e.g. text and images together.
choices.feedback: Right — multiple modalities like text, images, audio in one model.

choices.text: It runs in multiple languages.
choices.feedback: Many languages is still one modality (text). Multimodal spans types of input.

choices.text: It runs multiple copies at once.
choices.feedback: That's scaling, not modality — multimodal is about kinds of input.

multimodal.prompt: How does a multimodal model "see" an image you upload?

choices.text: The image is encoded into token-like vectors that share the same space as text tokens.
choices.feedback: Right — everything becomes vectors in a shared representation. To the transformer, image patches and words are the same kind of thing.

choices.text: A human describes the image to the model.
choices.feedback: No human needed — a vision encoder turns pixels into embeddings the language model can attend to directly.

choices.text: It runs OCR and reads only the text in the image.
choices.feedback: OCR alone would miss everything visual — the encoder captures objects, layout, and scenes, not just embedded text.

multimodal.prompt: Why is native multimodality more than a convenience feature?

choices.text: Some reasoning genuinely needs multiple senses at once — reading a chart, debugging a screenshot, describing a scene.
choices.feedback: Right — tasks like "why does this graph contradict the caption" can't decompose into separate text and vision calls.

choices.text: It's mostly marketing — text models could do it all.
choices.feedback: Text-only models literally can't inspect an image — piping images through captions loses the detail that reasoning needs.

choices.text: It makes models cheaper to run.
choices.feedback: Usually the opposite — vision adds compute. The win is capability: joint reasoning over what's seen and what's said.

choices.text: connect images and text — e.g. describe a photo or answer questions about it.
choices.feedback: Right — it ties what it 'sees' to language.

choices.text: only process text, never images.
choices.feedback: The 'vision' half means it handles images too.

choices.text: only generate images, never read them.
choices.feedback: It can interpret images, not just make them.

vision-language-models.prompt: A VLM answers questions about your chart. What's the rough pipeline?

choices.text: A vision encoder converts the image to embeddings; the language model attends over them alongside your question.
choices.feedback: Right — the chart becomes vectors in the model's working space, and attention connects your words to its regions.

choices.text: The chart is emailed to human annotators.
choices.feedback: It's all in-model and instant — the encoder-to-LLM handoff happens inside a single forward pass.

choices.text: The model searches the web for a similar chart.
choices.feedback: No search involved — it reads your actual image through its own vision encoder.

vision-language-models.prompt: Where do vision-language models still commonly stumble?

choices.text: Fine-grained details — precise counts, small text, exact spatial relationships.
choices.feedback: Right — the encoding compresses the image, and details slip through. Counting nine objects vs ten is genuinely hard for them.

choices.text: Recognizing famous landmarks.
choices.feedback: Landmarks are well-covered in training data — the harder failures are precise counting and fine spatial detail.

choices.text: Processing color images.
choices.feedback: Color is trivial — the trouble is precision: exact counts, tiny text, subtle layouts.

choices.text: Training a smaller "student" model to mimic a larger "teacher" model.
choices.feedback: Right — you get most of the quality in a cheaper, faster model.

choices.text: Removing water from the training data.
choices.feedback: It's a model-compression idea, nothing to do with literal distilling.

choices.text: Deleting the worst-performing layers.
choices.feedback: That's pruning — distillation trains a student to copy a teacher.

distillation.prompt: In distillation, why is learning from the teacher's full probability distribution better than learning from labels alone?

choices.text: The distribution carries the teacher's nuance — near-misses, confusable cases, relative confidence — that a hard label throws away.
choices.feedback: Right — "mostly cat, slightly fox" teaches more than "cat". That dark knowledge is what makes distillation work so well.

choices.text: Distributions are smaller files than labels.
choices.feedback: They're actually bigger — the value is informational: soft targets encode the teacher's judgment, not just its verdict.

choices.text: It isn't — labels work identically.
choices.feedback: Empirically the soft targets matter — students trained on them consistently beat students trained on labels alone.

distillation.prompt: Why do companies distill their frontier models?

choices.text: To get most of the capability at a fraction of the serving cost and latency.
choices.feedback: Right — the giant model is the teacher; the small one serves millions of users cheaply. Most production models you use are distilled.

choices.text: To hide the model from competitors.
choices.feedback: Secrecy isn't the driver — economics is. Small students serve traffic that big teachers can't afford to.

choices.text: Because regulators require small models.
choices.feedback: No such rule — the motive is cost and speed at serving time.

dpo.prompt: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) tunes a model using…

choices.text: pairs of preferred vs rejected answers, optimised directly without a separate reward model.
choices.feedback: Right — it skips RLHF's reward-model step and learns straight from preferences.

choices.text: a hand-written rulebook of correct answers.
choices.feedback: It learns from comparative preferences, not a fixed rulebook.

choices.text: more raw pretraining text.
choices.feedback: That's pretraining — DPO is preference alignment.

dpo.prompt: DPO and RLHF both use preference pairs. What does DPO cut out?

choices.text: The separate reward model and reinforcement-learning loop — it optimizes on preferences directly.
choices.feedback: Right — same goal, simpler machinery. That simplicity is why DPO spread fast through open-source fine-tuning.

choices.text: The need for any human input.
choices.feedback: Humans still supply the preference pairs — DPO removes the reward-model middleman, not the human judgment.

choices.text: The training data entirely.
choices.feedback: Data remains essential — DPO just uses it more directly, skipping the learned reward model and RL loop.

dpo.prompt: Why did DPO catch on so quickly in the open-source community?

choices.text: It delivers most of RLHF's benefit with a fraction of the engineering complexity and instability.
choices.feedback: Right — RL training is notoriously finicky. DPO reads like ordinary supervised fine-tuning, which small teams can actually run.

choices.text: It requires no GPUs.
choices.feedback: It still trains a model — GPUs required. The saving is complexity and stability, not hardware.

choices.text: It was the first method to align models.
choices.feedback: RLHF came first — DPO won mindshare by being dramatically simpler to implement, not by being first.

choices.text: further training a pretrained model on a narrower dataset to specialise it.
choices.feedback: Right — you start from a general model and adapt its weights.

choices.text: writing a longer, more detailed prompt.
choices.feedback: That's prompting — fine-tuning actually updates the weights.

choices.text: running the model on a faster GPU.
choices.feedback: Hardware doesn't specialise a model; training on new data does.

fine-tuning.prompt: When is fine-tuning the wrong tool?

choices.text: When the model just needs current or private facts — retrieval handles that better and cheaper.
choices.feedback: Right — fine-tuning shapes behavior and style; it's a poor way to inject knowledge that changes. RAG first, tune later.

choices.text: It's never wrong — always fine-tune.
choices.feedback: It's often overkill: prompting or retrieval solves most cases without training cost, drift risk, or maintenance burden.

choices.text: When you have too much training data.
choices.feedback: More data usually helps fine-tuning — the real misfit is using it for fresh facts, which retrieval serves better.

fine-tuning.prompt: What actually changes inside the model during fine-tuning?

choices.text: Its weights get further adjusted on your examples — the base knowledge stays, the behavior shifts.
choices.feedback: Right — you're continuing training, gently, on a narrow dataset. The model keeps its general ability but leans toward your patterns.

choices.text: A new prompt is permanently attached to it.
choices.feedback: That's system prompting. Fine-tuning goes deeper — the weights themselves move.

choices.text: It's rebuilt from scratch on your data alone.
choices.feedback: From-scratch training on a small dataset would produce a useless model — fine-tuning nudges an already-capable one.

choices.text: Quality degrades when models are trained repeatedly on AI-generated data.
choices.feedback: Right — errors compound as models learn from other models' output.

choices.text: The training server physically crashes.
choices.feedback: It's a data-quality spiral, not a hardware failure.

choices.text: The model forgets its own name.
choices.feedback: It's about degrading output quality across generations, not amnesia.

model-collapse.prompt: Why is model collapse described as a "photocopy of a photocopy" problem?

choices.text: Each generation trained on the previous one's output loses a little fidelity — rare patterns fade first, then quality broadly degrades.
choices.feedback: Right — the tails of the distribution vanish first. Recursive training without fresh data slowly forgets the unusual, then the true.

choices.text: Models are literally stored on photocopiers.
choices.feedback: It's an analogy — repeated copying compounds loss, and models trained on model output inherit and amplify each other's drift.

choices.text: Because photocopies are expensive.
choices.feedback: Cost isn't the point — information loss per generation is. Fidelity decays like copies of copies.

model-collapse.prompt: As AI-generated text floods the web, what challenge does that create for training future models?

choices.text: The web becomes partly model output, so future scrapes risk feeding models their own reflections.
choices.feedback: Right — clean human data becomes a scarcer resource, and labs now filter, date-stamp, and license data to keep training grounded.

choices.text: None — more text is always better.
choices.feedback: Volume isn't the issue; provenance is. Model-generated text in the pot risks the recursive-training decay that collapse describes.

choices.text: Websites will run out of storage.
choices.feedback: Storage is fine — the problem is data quality: distinguishing human signal from recycled model output.

quantization.prompt: What does quantization do to a model?

choices.text: Stores its weights at lower numerical precision to shrink size and speed it up.
choices.feedback: Right — e.g. 16-bit down to 4-bit, trading a little accuracy for efficiency.

choices.text: Adds more parameters to boost accuracy.
choices.feedback: The opposite — it compresses existing weights, it doesn't add any.

choices.text: Encrypts the weights for security.
choices.feedback: It reduces precision, not for secrecy but for size and speed.

quantization.prompt: Quantization shrinks a model 4x with only a small quality dip. What makes that possible?

choices.text: Weights don't need full precision — the patterns survive in coarser numbers.
choices.feedback: Right — a weight of 0.7312894 works almost as well stored as 0.73. Neural nets are remarkably tolerant of rounding.

choices.text: It deletes three-quarters of the weights.
choices.feedback: That's pruning — quantization keeps every weight but stores each in fewer bits.

choices.text: It compresses the training data.
choices.feedback: Training data isn't in the model — quantization shrinks the precision of the weights themselves.

quantization.prompt: Why does quantization matter for running models on your own laptop?

choices.text: It cuts memory needs enough that a model needing a datacenter GPU can fit in consumer RAM.
choices.feedback: Right — a 70B model at full precision needs ~140GB; at 4 bits, ~35GB. Quantization is the bridge to local AI.

choices.text: It makes the laptop's fan quieter.
choices.feedback: Heat may drop, but the real unlock is memory: fewer bits per weight means big models fit on small machines.

choices.text: It converts the model into a smartphone app.
choices.feedback: It's not packaging — it's numerical compression that slashes the memory footprint.

rlhf.prompt: What does RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) do?

choices.text: Tunes a model toward responses humans rated as better.
choices.feedback: Right — human preferences train a reward signal the model optimises for.

choices.text: Replaces all training data with human-written text.
choices.feedback: It uses preference ratings to fine-tune, not a wholesale data swap.

choices.text: Lets the model browse the internet live.
choices.feedback: That's retrieval/tools — RLHF is about aligning to human preferences.

rlhf.prompt: Why can't you just show a model examples of "good answers" and skip RLHF?

choices.text: Many qualities — helpfulness, tone, honesty — are easier for humans to compare than to write perfectly.
choices.feedback: Right — "which answer is better" is cheap, reliable human judgment; authoring ideal answers at scale isn't. RLHF turns comparisons into training signal.

choices.text: Good answers are copyrighted.
choices.feedback: Copyright isn't the obstacle — it's that judging is easier than authoring, so preference comparisons scale better than golden examples.

choices.text: You can — RLHF adds nothing.
choices.feedback: Supervised examples get you started, but preference training noticeably improves helpfulness and tone — it's why assistants stopped feeling like autocomplete.

rlhf.prompt: What's the role of the "reward model" in RLHF?

choices.text: It learns to predict human preferences, then stands in for humans as the training signal.
choices.feedback: Right — humans can't rate millions of outputs, so a model learns their taste and scores outputs at scale.

choices.text: It pays users a reward for good prompts.
choices.feedback: No payments involved — the "reward" is a score that guides the model toward outputs humans would prefer.

choices.text: It stores the model's factual knowledge.
choices.feedback: Facts live in the main model — the reward model only judges outputs, like a learned critic.

choices.text: How performance improves predictably as model size, data, and compute grow.
choices.feedback: Right — smooth, roughly power-law gains as you scale the inputs.

choices.text: How to scale a website's traffic.
choices.feedback: Different 'scaling' — these laws are about model performance vs resources.

choices.text: Legal limits on how large a model may be.
choices.feedback: They're empirical performance trends, not regulations.

scaling-laws.prompt: What made scaling laws so commercially important?

choices.text: They let labs predict a bigger model's performance before spending millions training it.
choices.feedback: Right — smooth, predictable curves turned "maybe bigger helps?" into an investable engineering plan. That confidence funded the scaling race.

choices.text: They proved small models are always sufficient.
choices.feedback: Nearly the opposite — they showed capability keeps climbing with scale, predictably enough to bet on.

choices.text: They made training free.
choices.feedback: Training stayed expensive — the laws made the expense predictable, which is what unlocked the investment.

scaling-laws.prompt: The Chinchilla result changed how labs train models. What did it show?

choices.text: Most models were too big for their data — a smaller model on more tokens uses the same compute better.
choices.feedback: Right — compute-optimal training balances parameters and data. Overnight, data became as strategic as model size.

choices.text: Models should always be as large as possible.
choices.feedback: It argued the opposite — many models were oversized and undertrained. Balance beats brute size.

choices.text: Scaling had permanently stopped working.
choices.feedback: Scaling kept working — Chinchilla refined the recipe, shifting emphasis toward more training data per parameter.

choices.text: data generated by a model or simulation rather than collected from the real world.
choices.feedback: Right — useful to fill gaps, but it can amplify a model's own biases.

choices.text: data stored in a fake database.
choices.feedback: It's about how the data was produced, not where it's stored.

choices.text: data that has been deleted.
choices.feedback: Synthetic means generated, not removed.

synthetic-data.prompt: Why would you train on model-generated data when real data exists?

choices.text: Real data can be scarce, private, or expensive — synthetic data can fill gaps, cover edge cases, and protect privacy.
choices.feedback: Right — rare medical cases, dangerous driving scenarios, private records: synthesis provides what collection can't.

choices.text: Synthetic data is always higher quality.
choices.feedback: Not always — it inherits the generator's blind spots. Its value is availability and coverage, not automatic superiority.

choices.text: Real data is illegal to use.
choices.feedback: Real data is used constantly — synthesis complements it where real examples are scarce, sensitive, or costly.

synthetic-data.prompt: What's the main danger of training on synthetic data at scale?

choices.text: Recycling model output into training can amplify the generator's errors and narrow diversity over generations.
choices.feedback: Right — the feedback loop is the risk. Done carelessly it drifts toward model collapse; done well, with filtering and real-data anchors, it's powerful.

choices.text: It costs more than hiring human writers.
choices.feedback: It's usually far cheaper — the danger is quality drift when models learn from their own reflections.

choices.text: There is no danger.
choices.feedback: There's a well-documented one: compounding biases and shrinking diversity when synthetic data feeds back untended.

training.prompt: What happens during "training" of a model?

choices.text: Its weights are adjusted over many examples to reduce prediction error.
choices.feedback: Right — repeated passes nudge the parameters toward better predictions.

choices.text: It memorises a fixed script of answers.
choices.feedback: It learns general patterns in weights, not a lookup script.

choices.text: It downloads a finished model from the internet.
choices.feedback: That's loading a model — training is the process that creates one.

training.prompt: Roughly how does a language model's training loop work?

choices.text: Predict the next token, measure the miss, nudge the weights, repeat — trillions of times.
choices.feedback: Right — the loop is almost embarrassingly simple. The magic is in the scale: trillions of tiny corrections add up to fluency.

choices.text: Engineers write out grammar rules and facts by hand.
choices.feedback: Nobody writes rules — the model absorbs patterns purely from prediction practice on enormous text.

choices.text: The model reads the internet once and remembers all of it.
choices.feedback: It doesn't memorize pages — it compresses patterns into weights through repeated predict-and-correct cycles.

training.prompt: Why does training a frontier model cost tens of millions of dollars?

choices.text: Licensing fees for the training data.
choices.feedback: Data costs exist, but the dominant expense is compute — thousands of GPUs running for months, plus the power to feed them.

choices.text: Months of time on thousands of GPUs, plus the electricity to run them.
choices.feedback: Right — the loop is simple but must run at planetary scale. Compute time is the overwhelming cost.

choices.text: Salaries for people who type the model's answers.
choices.feedback: Nobody types answers — the model learns from data automatically. The money burns in the datacenter.

choices.text: Asking the model to reason step by step before giving its answer.
choices.feedback: Right — laying out intermediate steps often improves hard answers.

choices.text: Chaining several separate models into a pipeline.
choices.feedback: That's a multi-model pipeline — chain-of-thought is one model reasoning aloud.

choices.text: Linking the model directly to a database.
choices.feedback: No database — it's about the model showing its working.

chain-of-thought.prompt: Why does "think step by step" improve accuracy on multi-step problems?

choices.text: Each generated step becomes context for the next, letting the model build toward the answer instead of leaping to it.
choices.feedback: Right — the model computes in its own output. Writing the intermediate steps is the model's working memory.

choices.text: It's a magic phrase that unlocks hidden abilities.
choices.feedback: Not magic — mechanics. Generated steps become context the model conditions on, which is what enables multi-step accuracy.

choices.text: It makes the model try harder emotionally.
choices.feedback: No effort dial exists — the benefit is structural: intermediate tokens carry intermediate results forward.

chain-of-thought.prompt: Is a model's written chain of thought a faithful record of how it computed the answer?

choices.text: Not necessarily — the prose can be a plausible story while the real computation happened elsewhere in the network.
choices.feedback: Right — helpful and legible isn't the same as faithful. Researchers actively study when stated reasoning diverges from actual computation.

choices.text: Yes — it's a literal printout of its internal process.
choices.feedback: The text is generated like any other output — it can rationalize rather than report. Faithfulness is an open research question.

choices.text: Models never show their reasoning.
choices.feedback: They readily produce reasoning text — the subtle question is whether that text reflects the underlying computation.

choices.text: output a structured request to run a tool or API, then use the result.
choices.feedback: Right — the model picks the function and arguments; your code runs it.

choices.text: rewrite its own source code.
choices.feedback: It calls external tools, it doesn't edit itself.

choices.text: train itself on new data.
choices.feedback: Calling a function isn't training — no weights change.

function-calling.prompt: When a model "calls a function", what does it actually output?

choices.text: Structured text naming the function and its arguments — your code executes it and returns the result.
choices.feedback: Right — the model never runs anything. It emits a request; the surrounding system does the deed and feeds back the result.
